About.title: Why

paragraphs.one: I spent my whole life looking for answers. Something was not right, I knew it, but nobody could tell me what it was. Not school, not doctors, not the system. I eventually found an answer through international content creators who openly talked about ADHD in adults. It was a turning point.
paragraphs.two: That's when I realised: this kind of content simply did not exist in Slovakia. Adults with ADHD had nowhere to look for information in Slovak, there were few specialists, and the myth that “ADHD only affects children” was still alive – even among healthcare professionals.
paragraphs.three: I founded ADHD Slovakia to help people find answers sooner than I did. I write articles based on scientific sources, help people navigate the system and advocate for the rights of adults with ADHD in Slovakia.
paragraphs.four: Thanks to this community, more than 10 adults have already successfully received a diagnosis confirmed by a professional. Each of them experienced a similar moment to mine – finally getting an answer.

positive.title: Positive screening
positive.text: You scored above the threshold in the {categories} category. This is intended solely as an indicative screening tool. We recommend discussing the results with a clinical psychologist or psychiatrist.

negative.title: Negative screening
negative.text: Your current score is below the threshold for an indicative suspicion of ADHD in adults.

questions.A1: Do you have difficulty maintaining attention on tasks that require prolonged concentration?
questions.A2: Do you often forget everyday essentials (keys, wallet, phone)?
questions.A3: When someone is talking to you, do you often find your thoughts elsewhere and miss part of the sentence?
questions.A4: Do you have problems organizing tasks and managing time — often missing deadlines?
questions.A5: Do you avoid tasks that require prolonged mental effort?
questions.A6: Do you lose things needed for activities (tools, documents, phone)?
questions.A7: Are you often distracted by external stimuli that pull you away from a task?
questions.A8: Do you forget scheduled appointments or deadlines?
questions.A9: Do you have problems finishing details — starting many things but completing few?
questions.B1: Do you often move your hands/feet or have difficulty sitting still?
questions.B2: Do you feel uncomfortable when you have to sit in one place for a long time?
questions.B3: Do you often start answering before someone has finished their question?
questions.B4: Do you have difficulty waiting your turn — for example in a queue or during a conversation?
questions.B5: Do you often interrupt others or intrude into other people's conversations?
questions.B6: Do you do things impulsively without thinking about the consequences?
questions.B7: Do you feel that your mind is like a “motor that never stops”?
questions.B8: Do you often talk too much or very quickly?
questions.B9: Do you seek intense stimulation (extreme sports, games) because ordinary things bore you?

examples.A1: e.g. reading documents, filling out forms
examples.B2: e.g. during meetings, at the cinema, while travelling

whatIsAdhd.title: What is ADHD?
whatIsAdhd.content:
ADHD, or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that interfere with everyday functioning. These symptoms usually appear in childhood and may persist into adulthood.

It is not an excuse or the result of poor parenting — it reflects differences in how the brain functions, with measurable neurological differences.

symptoms.title: ADHD symptoms
symptoms.content:
ADHD symptoms are divided into two main categories:

Inattention:
• Difficulty concentrating on tasks
• Time blindness — difficulty estimating time
• Chronic procrastination
• Reduced working memory
• Hyperfocus on interesting topics

Hyperactivity and impulsivity:
• Inner restlessness and difficulty staying still
• Interrupting others and making hasty decisions
• Emotional dysregulation — rapid and intense emotions

children.title: ADHD in children
children.content:
In children, ADHD is often most visible externally — in behaviour, motor activity and social interactions. It is not a sign of poor upbringing or low intelligence.

Typical signs in children:
• Constant movement and difficulty sitting still
• Impulsive behaviour without considering consequences
• Forgetting school supplies and responsibilities
• Difficulties in groups due to emotional reactions

The key is understanding and a firm, supportive structure — not punishment.

adults.title: ADHD in adults
adults.content:
ADHD does not simply disappear after adolescence. Many adults are diagnosed only after they begin experiencing problems at work, in relationships or with managing everyday life.

In adults, hyperactivity often becomes more internal restlessness. Common difficulties include:
• Chronic lateness and missed deadlines
• Difficulty maintaining work or relationships
• A lifelong feeling that something is not right
• Low self-esteem after years of difficulties

causes.title: Causes of ADHD
causes.content:
ADHD has a strong genetic component — heritability estimates are above 70%. It is not caused by poor parenting, sugar or screens.

Biological factors:
• Genetics — having a parent with ADHD substantially increases the child's risk
• Differences in dopamine and noradrenaline signalling in the brain
• Differences in the development of the prefrontal cortex

Risk factors:
• Smoking or alcohol exposure during pregnancy
• Low birth weight and premature birth
• Exposure to heavy metals in early childhood

diagnosis.title: ADHD diagnosis
diagnosis.content:
ADHD diagnosis is a comprehensive process — there is no single test or blood test that can diagnose it. It is based on a detailed clinical and psychological assessment.

Diagnosis may include:
• Detailed developmental history from childhood
• Standardized questionnaires and rating scales
• Psychological testing of cognitive functions
• Ruling out other possible causes (anxiety, depression, trauma)

In Slovakia, diagnosis is carried out by a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist. The path to diagnosis can be long because there are relatively few specialists.

treatment.title: Treatment and therapy
treatment.content:
The most effective approach often combines several components:

Medication (prescribed by a psychiatrist):
• Stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) — affect dopamine and noradrenaline signalling
• Non-stimulant medication (atomoxetine) — an option when stimulants are unsuitable or ineffective

Therapy:
• Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
• ADHD-focused coaching
• Training in executive functioning skills

Lifestyle:
• Regular physical activity, sleep hygiene and a structured routine

school.title: ADHD at school
school.content:
The school environment can be a major challenge for children with ADHD — it requires exactly the skills that may be most difficult for them.

Common difficulties:
• Difficulty filtering out distracting stimuli
• Forgetting school supplies and homework
• Impulsive behaviour in groups

What can help:
• Sitting near the front and away from windows
• Breaking tasks into smaller steps
• Allowing appropriate movement breaks
• Praising effort, not only results

work.title: ADHD at work
work.content:
Adults with ADHD can be highly productive when they are in an environment that suits their needs.

Challenges:
• Procrastination on uninteresting tasks
• Forgetting verbal agreements
• Difficulties with open-office environments
• Impulsive reactions to criticism

Potential strengths:
• Hyperfocus on interesting projects
• Creativity and unconventional solutions
• Performing well in crisis situations

Helpful strategies may include flexible schedules, remote work, digital planners and noise-cancelling headphones.

relationships.title: Relationships and ADHD
relationships.content:
ADHD can affect close relationships — romantic, family and friendships.

Common difficulties:
• Forgetting promises and agreements
• Appearing not to listen during conversations
• Emotional intensity and sensitivity to criticism (RSD)
• Uneven distribution of responsibilities at home

What can help:
• Written agreements instead of relying only on verbal agreements
• Shared digital calendars
• Understanding that forgetfulness does not necessarily mean a lack of interest
• Couples therapy with a professional familiar with ADHD

lifestyle.title: Lifestyle
lifestyle.content:
A healthy lifestyle can help manage some ADHD symptoms.

Physical activity:
• May support mood and attention regulation
• May help reduce restlessness and improve concentration
• Consistency and individual tolerance are important

Sleep:
• Insufficient sleep can worsen symptoms
• A consistent sleep schedule can help, including on weekends
• Limiting screens before bedtime may be useful

Diet:
• A balanced diet with sufficient protein and fibre
• Limiting excessive intake of simple sugars
• A varied diet containing sources of omega-3 fatty acids

Routine:
• A structured daily routine can reduce cognitive load
• Visual planners and reminders can help

faq.title: FAQ
faq.content:
Frequently asked questions about ADHD:

Is ADHD a real diagnosis?
Yes. ADHD is a scientifically recognized neurodevelopmental disorder.

Can ADHD be cured?
ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder that can persist into adulthood. Treatment and support can significantly improve functioning and quality of life.

Can adults have ADHD?
Yes. Many people are diagnosed only in adulthood.

Is ADHD caused by poor parenting?
No. ADHD has a substantial genetic and neurobiological component.

Can medication help?
For many people, yes. A doctor decides whether medication is appropriate based on an individual assessment.
